title: Atomic commit across machines: two-phase commit and XA
goal: By the end you can explain why one machine's commit doesn't extend to two, run two-phase commit by hand with PREPARE TRANSACTION, say what an in-doubt participant must do when its coordinator dies and what that costs, judge when XA, a Percolator-style commit or a saga fits, and build a coordinator that recovers from its own log.

warmup.q: A coordinator has prepared a transfer on two PostgreSQL servers, and both voted yes. It wrote COMMIT to its log, sent COMMIT PREPARED to the first server, and crashed before reaching the second. What does the second server do with the transfer and its row lock?
options: Rolls it back after a timeout, so its row lock is released
Commits it on its own after a timeout, since it voted yes
Keeps it prepared and keeps the row lock until someone tells it the outcome, even across a restart
Asks the first server for the outcome and commits, because PostgreSQL servers coordinate this themselves
warmup.why: A participant that voted yes has promised to commit if told to, so it can't roll back on its own, and it can't commit on its own because it doesn't know the decision: maybe the coordinator decided abort. It waits, holding its locks, and a prepared transaction survives a restart. Rolling back after a timeout is the tempting answer, and here it would leave the first server's debit committed with no credit. PostgreSQL servers don't talk to each other about prepared transactions; only the coordinator, or a person, finishes them.

sections.h: One machine commits with one write; two machines have no such write
sections.body:
Lesson 1 put the commit at one moment: the commit record reaching the write-ahead log on disk. A crash before that moment undoes everything; a crash after it undoes nothing. One disk, one record, one moment. Every lesson since has been about what concurrent transactions see around that moment. This lesson asks a different question: what if the transaction's rows live on two machines?

Here is the case. A wallet service keeps customer wallets in its own PostgreSQL server, `wallets`. A settlement service keeps what the platform owes each merchant in another server, `payouts`. A coffee purchase moves 30.00 from wallet w-17 to the merchant m-cafe: a debit on `wallets`, a credit on `payouts`. Both must happen, or neither. No single disk holds both rows, so no single commit record can cover both.

Version 1 commits one, then the other: debit w-17 and COMMIT, then credit m-cafe and COMMIT. Now list what can happen between the two commits. The credit can break a constraint on `payouts`. The network to `payouts` can drop. `payouts` can crash before its commit record reaches disk. The service running the transfer can be killed during a deploy. Each time, the customer has paid 30.00 and the merchant got nothing. The Try it does exactly this.

Can you undo the debit? Not safely. Once `wallets` has committed, other transactions have seen the new balance and acted on it: a fraud check approved the next purchase against 70.00. A credit that puts the money back is a new transaction, not an undo, and it can fail too.

Version 2 sends both commits at the same moment. That shrinks the window but doesn't close it: one server can still say no, or die, while the other says yes.

The fix needs two ideas. First, nobody commits until everybody has promised that they can: each server does all its work, checks every constraint, makes its changes durable, and only then gives up its right to say no. Second, one place records the decision durably before anyone is told. **Every participant promises, one durable record decides, then everyone commits.** That is the picture for this lesson, and it has a name: two-phase commit.

try.title: Lose 30.00 between two commits
steps: From the `labs` folder, start PostgreSQL with `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait` and open a prompt: `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz`. One server stands in for two machines: PostgreSQL can't run one transaction across two databases, so `wallets` and `payouts` are as separate as two servers.
Run the setup, then the transfer. `\c` closes the current connection and opens a new one. When it closes `payouts` before the COMMIT, that is the settlement service dying mid-transfer.
Predict both balances before you read them.

code.title: one psql session

try.expect:
```text
 balance_minor
---------------
          7000
(1 row)

You are now connected to database "payouts" as user "sfz".
 balance_minor
---------------
             0
(1 row)
```

(Setup output trimmed.) The debit committed on `wallets`. The credit was still in an open transaction when its connection closed, so PostgreSQL rolled it back, exactly as it would after a crash. The customer paid 30.00 and the merchant got nothing, and neither server did anything wrong: each kept its own promise about its own data.

refs.title: PostgreSQL 18: Reliability and the write-ahead log

sections.h: Two-phase commit: every participant promises, then one log line decides
sections.body:
Two-phase commit (2PC) has two roles. The **coordinator** runs the transaction and decides its outcome. It is often a library inside your own service, called a transaction manager. The **participants** are the servers that hold the data. The transaction gets one global id, here `txf-1`.

Phase one is prepare. The coordinator sends each participant its statements, then asks it to prepare. A participant that can commit writes all its changes, plus a record saying "prepared", to its write-ahead log, flushes it to disk, and answers yes. That yes is a promise: whatever happens next, even a crash and a restart, it will commit if told to. So it may no longer abort on its own, and it keeps every lock the transaction took. A participant that can't commit (a constraint failed, it ran out of disk) rolls back and answers no.

Then the coordinator decides. If every answer is yes, it appends `txf-1 COMMIT` to its own log and flushes that to disk. **That one log line is the commit point** of the whole distributed transaction. If any answer is no, or an answer doesn't arrive in time, it decides abort.

Phase two is commit. The coordinator tells every participant the outcome. After a commit decision it keeps retrying each participant until each one confirms, for minutes or days if it must, because it can't take the decision back. The stepper walks through both outcomes.

Notice the two points of no return. A participant's yes takes away its right to abort. The coordinator's log line takes away everyone's right to abort. An abort needs no log line at all: a transaction the log doesn't mention is treated as aborted (presumed abort), which is safe because nobody can have committed without that line.

PostgreSQL implements the participant side. `PREPARE TRANSACTION 'txf-1@wallets'` ends your session's transaction without finishing it: the transaction lives on as a prepared transaction, listed in `pg_prepared_xacts`, holding its locks. Later, any session connected to the same database finishes it with `COMMIT PREPARED` or `ROLLBACK PREPARED`. The feature is off by default (`max_prepared_transactions = 0`), changing that setting needs a restart, and the docs say it isn't meant for application code: it is for transaction managers. In the Try its each participant gets its own gid, because both databases sit on one server and a gid must be unique on the whole server; XA does the same with a branch qualifier.

Count the cost. A local commit is one round trip and one flush. Two-phase commit needs two round trips to every participant and three flushes in a row on the commit path: the participants' prepare records (in parallel), the coordinator's decision, then the participants' commit records. Across two regions, at about 70 ms a round trip, that is about 140 ms of network time on every commit instead of 70.

steps: In the psql prompt (in `wallets`), try to prepare a transaction. It fails, and the failed PREPARE rolls the transaction back. Switch the feature on and restart the server from the `labs` folder: `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml restart db`.

Run phase two: commit each prepared transaction. Note that terminal 1 commits from a new statement after its own transaction ended: any session in the right database can finish a prepared transaction.

HINT:  Set "max_prepared_transactions" to a nonzero value.

---------------+----------+-------------------------------

(2 rows)

sections.h: If the coordinator dies, participants wait in doubt and keep their locks
sections.body:
Now the failure the protocol was built around. Both servers voted yes, and then the coordinator's process dies before it tells anyone the outcome. Look at it from `payouts`. It promised to commit if told to, and nobody is telling it anything. Such a participant is **in doubt**.

Can it decide on its own? From where `payouts` sits, it can't see what happened elsewhere. Committing is unsafe: for all it knows, `wallets` voted no or answered too late, and the coordinator decided abort. Aborting is unsafe too: maybe the coordinator wrote COMMIT and `wallets` has already committed. Asking `wallets` helps only sometimes. If `wallets` has committed, `payouts` can commit too; if `wallets` is also just prepared, neither knows whether the log line exists. So an in-doubt participant waits for the coordinator. Two-phase commit is a **blocking** protocol: one dead coordinator can stop the participants indefinitely.

While it waits, it holds its locks. The Try it shows what that means on PostgreSQL. Plain reads still work: under MVCC, from lesson 4, they see the last committed version. But every writer that touches an in-doubt row, w-17 on `wallets` or m-cafe on `payouts`, queues behind the prepared transaction until its own `lock_timeout` fires. m-cafe is a merchant: every purchase at that cafe would queue. `pg_blocking_pids` reports the blocker as process 0, because a prepared transaction belongs to no session, and there is no session to kill. VACUUM can't remove dead row versions newer than the prepared transaction, since lesson 4's horizon can't pass a transaction that is still running. Restarting the database doesn't help either: the prepared transaction is on disk, comes back at startup with its locks, and the log says so (`recovering prepared transaction 767`).

How long does this last? As long as the coordinator is gone. If it restarts in 20 seconds, that is 20 seconds of locked rows. If its disk is gone, it lasts until a person picks an outcome by hand, what XA calls a heuristic decision. A person who guesses wrong breaks atomicity: one side committed, the other rolled back.

So recovery is the coordinator's first job when it starts. It reads its log, asks every participant for its in-doubt gids (`pg_prepared_xacts` in PostgreSQL), commits the ones its log says COMMIT, and rolls back the rest. That is the lab. It works only if the log never forgets a decision it acted on. If the COMMIT line wasn't flushed before the first `COMMIT PREPARED` went out, a crash can lose the line after one side committed, and recovery would roll back the other side. That is why the lab's `recordCommit` calls `force(true)` before it returns.

steps: Terminals 1 and 2 play the coordinator again, and this time it dies after phase one: prepare `txf-2` on both, and don't commit. Open terminal 3 on `wallets` and update w-17. It waits.
In terminal 1, find out who it waits for, then make some dead row versions on w-18 and vacuum. Predict whether VACUUM can remove them. Watch terminal 3 give up after 10 seconds.

Restart the server from the `labs` folder (`docker compose -f env/postgres.yml restart db`), reconnect terminal 1 and check `pg_prepared_xacts` again. Then resolve both as the coordinator's log would: commit.

sections.h: XA runs two-phase commit across products, and most teams avoid it
sections.body:
So far both participants were PostgreSQL. In your services the second participant is often another product: an Oracle ledger and an IBM MQ queue, or PostgreSQL and ActiveMQ. Two-phase commit across different products needs a shared interface, and the standard one is **X/Open XA**, from 1991. XA isn't a network protocol. It is an API between a transaction manager and each resource, which the vendor's driver implements over its own wire protocol.

In Java, XA appears as JTA. Each resource gives the transaction manager an `XAResource` with `start`, `end`, `prepare`, `commit`, `rollback` and `recover`. Every branch is named by an `Xid`: a format id, a global transaction id and a branch qualifier, the same "one id per participant" idea as `txf-1@wallets`. In Quarkus, the `quarkus-narayana-jta` extension runs Narayana as the transaction manager inside your service, writes its decisions to a log directory on local disk, and starts a recovery service when it detects XA data sources. pgJDBC's `PGXADataSource` turns `prepare` into `PREPARE TRANSACTION`. The Try it runs both phases by hand and then recovers, as Narayana would after a restart.

Most teams that try XA in production end up avoiding it, for four reasons.

1. The coordinator is your service process, and its log sits on that pod's disk. Kubernetes reschedules the pod with a fresh disk, the log is gone, and the in-doubt branches in Oracle wait for a DBA to make a heuristic decision.
2. Each resource sees only its own locks. If transaction A holds a row in Oracle and waits for a row in PostgreSQL that transaction B holds, while B waits for A's Oracle row, neither database sees a cycle. Lesson 5's deadlock detector never fires; a timeout ends it. The same blindness rules out SSI across products, since no database sees the other's read-write dependencies.
3. Every transaction pays the extra round trips and flushes, and every lock is held until the slowest participant has prepared.
4. Much of what you need to change doesn't speak XA at all: Redis, DynamoDB, a card issuer's HTTP API, an email. Kafka has an accepted proposal to take part in two-phase commit, KIP-939, but as of November 2026 it hasn't shipped in a release.

What about removing the blocking? Three-phase commit (3PC) adds a round so that a participant that hears nothing can decide on its own after a timeout. That is safe only if every message and every pause has a known upper bound. Real networks and real processes have no such bound, which the Faults, time and truth track shows: a slow coordinator looks exactly like a dead one, and two participants that time out differently can decide differently. Instead of 3PC, systems that need atomic commit make the coordinator itself survive crashes, by replicating its log with consensus. The Consistency and consensus track builds that machinery.

try.title: Run XA by hand, then recover
steps: This uses the `wallets` and `payouts` databases from the earlier Try its, with prepared transactions switched on. Read `XaDemo.kt`. It runs `start`, the UPDATE, `end` and `prepare` on each database, closes its connections without committing (the coordinator dies), and then plays the restarted transaction manager: `recover` on each resource, then `commit`.
Before you run it, predict what the gids in `pg_prepared_xacts` look like: the demo's Xid has format id 1001, global id `txf-7` and the database name as the branch.
Run it from the `labs` folder. Then run it a second time: is there anything left from the first run to recover?

code.title: XaDemo.kt (the two phases)

try.expect:
```text
== phase 1: start, work, end and prepare each branch of txf-7
wallets  prepare -> XA_OK, a yes vote
payouts  prepare -> XA_OK, a yes vote
== what PostgreSQL holds now
payouts  1001_dHhmLTc=_cGF5b3V0cw==
wallets  1001_dHhmLTc=_d2FsbGV0cw==
== recovery: a restarted transaction manager asks each resource what is in doubt
wallets  in doubt: formatId 1001, global id txf-7, branch wallets
wallets  commit -> done
payouts  in doubt: formatId 1001, global id txf-7, branch payouts
payouts  commit -> done
w-17 is now 2500
```

pgJDBC writes the Xid into the gid as the format id, then the global id and the branch in Base64 (`dHhmLTc=` is `txf-7`), and `recover` decodes them again from `pg_prepared_xacts`. That listing is all a restarted transaction manager learns from the database. Whether to commit has to come from its own log; this demo just commits. The second run recovers only its own branches, since the first run left nothing behind, and w-17 reads `1000`. Each run moves 15.00.

refs.title: Quarkus: using transactions (Narayana, XA and recovery)

sections.h: Two ways around the coordinator: put the decision in the data, or give up atomic commit
sections.body:
The weak spot of two-phase commit is the coordinator: a separate process holding the one record that decides, which participants must wait for. There are two ways around it.

The first moves the decision into the data. Google's Percolator (2010) added transactions to Bigtable, which can only change one row atomically. A Percolator transaction locks every cell it writes, and picks one lock as the **primary**; every other lock stores a pointer to it. To commit, the client replaces the primary lock with a commit record, in one single-row atomic write. That write is the commit point, doing the job of our log line, but stored next to the data where any reader can find it. The client then cleans up the other locks. If the client dies first, the next reader that meets a leftover lock follows the pointer to the primary. A commit record there means roll the lock forward; no commit record and an abandoned primary means roll it back. Nobody waits for a coordinator to return, because there is no separate coordinator. The price is paid elsewhere: a transaction that runs into a dead client's lock must clean it up first, and the paper says this lazy cleanup can delay a commit by tens of seconds. That was fine for building Google's web index and would be far too slow for payments. Percolator gives snapshot isolation, so lesson 3's write skew is possible. TiDB's storage layer, TiKV, uses a Percolator-style protocol. The Consistency and consensus track's lesson on distributed SQL shows how Spanner and CockroachDB keep two-phase commit and replicate every coordinator and participant with consensus.

The second gives up atomic commit and keeps the business rule. The Encoding, APIs and workflows track's lesson on durable execution covered workflows that survive crashes. A **saga**, an idea from Garcia-Molina and Salem in 1987, is such a workflow made of local transactions, each with a compensating step. The transfer becomes: debit w-17 and record the transfer as pending, in one local transaction on `wallets`; credit m-cafe with a payout entry keyed by the transfer id, in one local transaction on `payouts`; mark the transfer done. If the credit can never succeed, the compensation refunds w-17. Each step commits alone, so nothing is in doubt and no lock outlives its step. Each step is idempotent, so the workflow engine can retry it safely.

What you give up is isolation. Between the steps, anyone can see the debit without the credit: lesson 1's dirty read, at business scale. And a compensation is a new action, not a rollback: the refund shows on the customer's statement, and an email already sent stays sent. So model "pending" as a real state that reports and support staff understand.

Choose by where the participants live. Inside one distributed database, let its built-in commit protocol do the work. Across services and products, use a saga with idempotency keys. Use XA only when every participant supports it, the coordinator's log is durable and backed up, and contention is low.

refs.title: Peng and Dabek: Large-scale incremental processing using distributed transactions and notifications (Percolator, OSDI 2010)

analogy: Two-phase commit works like a property sale with an escrow agent. The agent asks the seller to sign the deed and the buyer to deposit the money, and once each has done so, neither can back out on their own: the signed deed and the deposit sit with the agent. When both are in, the agent stamps the file "closed", and from that stamp the sale has happened, even before the deed is registered and the money is paid out. If the agent vanishes after collecting both, the seller can't sell the house to anyone else and the buyer can't touch the money, because neither knows whether the file was stamped: they are in doubt. The analogy breaks on what the waiting costs. Real people would call a lawyer within a day, while an in-doubt database transaction blocks every writer of its rows the whole time, and a person who resolves it by guessing can leave the money paid on one side only.
in_your_world: In a Quarkus service with `quarkus-narayana-jta`, a `@Transactional` method that touches an Oracle data source and a JMS queue, both XA, is two-phase commit with Narayana as the coordinator, and its log lives in the object store directory on the pod's disk. If the pod dies after prepare, Oracle keeps the rows locked until Narayana's recovery service comes back with the same log, which means a persistent volume and a stable node identifier, or a DBA resolves it from `DBA_2PC_PENDING`. Most payment teams avoid this path: the Oracle write and an outbox row commit in one local transaction, a relay publishes the event to Kafka, and multi-service flows such as authorize, capture and settle run as sagas in Temporal, with each step an idempotent local transaction keyed by the payment id. Keep XA for the rare case where every participant supports it and you can guarantee the coordinator's log survives.
mistake: The common mistake is to treat a prepared or XA transaction like an ordinary one that a timeout will clean up. A team sees a row locked for an hour, finds a prepared transaction in `pg_prepared_xacts` or `DBA_2PC_PENDING`, and rolls it back to free the row. If the coordinator had already decided to commit and the other participant had committed, the transfer is now half done and nothing will ever report it. People do it because the lock is visible and urgent while the coordinator's log is out of sight. The fix: before resolving anything by hand, read the coordinator's log or check what the other participants did with the same global id, and pick that outcome; prevent it by keeping the coordinator's log on durable, backed-up storage and alerting on prepared transactions older than a minute.

compare.title: One transfer two ways: two-phase commit and a saga

a.label: Two-phase commit
a.title: one distributed transaction
a.src:
wallets: BEGIN, debit w-17           lock w-17
payouts: BEGIN, credit m-cafe        lock m-cafe
wallets: PREPARE  -> yes             w-17 still locked
payouts: PREPARE  -> yes             m-cafe still locked
coordinator log: txf-1 COMMIT        <- commit point
wallets: COMMIT PREPARED             w-17 released
payouts: COMMIT PREPARED             m-cafe released

coordinator dies after prepare:  both rows stay locked
isolation:  nobody sees a debit without its credit*
needs:      XA or PREPARE on every participant

b.label: Saga
b.title: three local transactions in a workflow
b.src:
wallets: debit w-17, transfer txf-1 = pending   commit
payouts: credit m-cafe, entry txf-1             commit
wallets: transfer txf-1 = done                  commit
if the credit can never succeed:
wallets: refund w-17, txf-1 = refunded          commit

workflow dies between steps:  it resumes; nothing locked
isolation:  anyone can see txf-1 pending
needs:      idempotent steps and a durable workflow

compare.note: Two-phase commit keeps the transfer atomic and holds locks across both servers until the end, so a dead coordinator freezes rows. A saga commits each step at once, so nothing is ever in doubt and nothing stays locked, but the in-between state is visible and undoing means a new step, a refund, rather than a rollback. *Even 2PC shows half the transfer for a moment to a reader of both servers, between the two COMMIT PREPAREDs, as the stepper showed.

worked.title: Recover after a crash: decide every in-doubt branch

steps.say: Gather what the restarted coordinator can see: its own log, and the prepared transactions on each participant.
steps.code:
coordinator.log           wallets: pg_prepared_xacts      payouts: pg_prepared_xacts
txf-4 COMMIT              txf-5@wallets                   txf-5@payouts
txf-5 COMMIT              txf-6@wallets                   txf-6@payouts
                          batch-9@ledger

steps.say: Apply one rule per gid. Our gids end with `@<participant>`. A COMMIT line for the transfer id means commit. No line means the coordinator never decided commit, so no participant can have committed, and rolling back is safe. A gid from another coordinator is not ours to touch.
steps.code:
txf-5@wallets    log says COMMIT     -> COMMIT PREPARED
txf-6@wallets    no line             -> ROLLBACK PREPARED   (presumed abort)
batch-9@ledger   not ours            -> leave it alone
txf-5@payouts    log says COMMIT     -> COMMIT PREPARED
txf-6@payouts    no line             -> ROLLBACK PREPARED
txf-4            nothing prepared    -> already finished before the crash

steps.say: Write it as code. The loop is short because the hard part, deciding, was done before the crash and written down.

Check why the order of operations in `run` makes this safe. The COMMIT line is flushed after every yes and before the first COMMIT PREPARED. If the coordinator flushed after sending commits, a crash could lose the line while one side had committed, and this loop would roll the other side back.
steps.code:
safe:    prepare all -> fsync "txf-5 COMMIT" -> COMMIT PREPARED wallets -> COMMIT PREPARED payouts
unsafe:  prepare all -> COMMIT PREPARED wallets -> crash (line never written)
         recovery: no line for txf-5 -> ROLLBACK PREPARED txf-5@payouts -> half a transfer

lab.title: Build a two-phase commit coordinator that survives its own crash
steps: Run the tests from the `labs` folder. They start a PostgreSQL 18 container of their own with `max_prepared_transactions = 10` and two databases, `wallets` and `payouts` (a few seconds, more on the first pull). All 10 fail.

Read `TwoPhaseCommit.kt`. `Participant`, `DecisionLog`, `CrashPoint` and `maybeCrash` are provided. `CoordinatorCrashed` extends `Error`, so a `catch (e: Exception)` can't hide a crash, just as no catch block runs when a process is killed.

Write `Coordinator.run` from its KDoc: phase one with `BEGIN`, the statements and `PREPARE TRANSACTION` on each participant; on a no vote, `ROLLBACK` and `ROLLBACK PREPARED`; then the log line, then `COMMIT PREPARED`, with the three `maybeCrash` calls. Four tests pass, including the one that checks a writer gets SQLSTATE 55P03 on a row an in-doubt transaction holds.
Write `Coordinator.recover`. Four more pass: after a crash before the decision, after it, between the two commits, and with another coordinator's gid on the same server.
Fix `in_doubt.sql`. It runs, and its numbers are wrong in three ways. The last two tests pass.
hints: Catch only `SQLException` in phase one. `e.sqlState` gives `23505` for the duplicate payout entry and `23514` for the CHECK on the wallet balance.
After a failed statement inside BEGIN, `ROLLBACK` ends the aborted transaction. After a failed PREPARE, PostgreSQL has already rolled back, and a ROLLBACK only warns, so you can send it either way.
In `recover`, `p.preparedGids()` already filters to the participant's own database; you still have to keep only the gids that end with `@${p.name}`.

`in_doubt.sql`: the join must be a LEFT JOIN, so a transaction nobody waits for keeps its row; count `w.pid`, not `*`; skip granted locks (`NOT w.granted`), because each prepared transaction holds its own transaction id lock; and keep `p.database = current_database()`.

drill.title: The coordinator's commit path from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write `run(txId, work)` for a coordinator over PostgreSQL participants: phase one, the abort path, the decision and phase two. Then answer: what is the commit point, and why must it come before the first `COMMIT PREPARED`?

recap: One machine commits with one record on one disk. Across two machines no single write covers both, so commit-one-then-the-other loses money whenever the second side fails.

Two-phase commit: every participant prepares (changes durable, locks kept, votes yes or no), the coordinator flushes one COMMIT line to its log (the commit point), then tells everyone. No line means abort.
PostgreSQL is a participant: `PREPARE TRANSACTION 'gid'`, `pg_prepared_xacts`, then `COMMIT PREPARED` or `ROLLBACK PREPARED` from the same database. `max_prepared_transactions` is 0 by default.

A participant whose coordinator died is in doubt: it can't decide alone, keeps its row locks across restarts, blocks writers and holds back VACUUM. Recovery reads the log and finishes every in-doubt gid.

XA is 2PC across products (JTA and Narayana in Java). Its log on a pod's disk, cross-system deadlocks nobody detects and the many systems without XA make teams avoid it. 3PC needs bounded delays that real networks don't give.

Percolator moves the commit point into the data (a primary lock), so any reader can finish a dead client's transaction. A saga gives up atomic commit for local steps with compensations, and pays with visible in-between states.

quiz.q: A coordinator crashes after both participants voted yes but before it wrote anything to its log. It restarts with its log intact. What does recovery do with the two prepared branches?
options: Commits both: every participant voted yes, so the transfer can go through
Rolls back both: with no COMMIT line, the coordinator never decided commit, so nobody can have committed
Leaves both prepared and waits for an operator
Commits the one that prepared first and rolls back the other
quiz.why: Presumed abort: the COMMIT line is written only after all yes votes and before any COMMIT PREPARED, so its absence proves no participant committed. Rolling back both is consistent with every participant. Committing both would also be atomic here, which makes it tempting, but recovery can't tell this case from one where a third vote never arrived, so the rule has to be abort. Waiting for an operator throws away the information the log gives.

quiz.q: A payments database shows a prepared transaction `txf-5@payouts` that has held a merchant's row for an hour. A DBA runs `ROLLBACK PREPARED 'txf-5@payouts'` to unblock checkouts. The coordinator's log says `txf-5 COMMIT`, and `txf-5@wallets` committed an hour ago. What is the result?
options: Nothing bad: the coordinator will notice and commit it again
The whole transfer is rolled back on both servers
Half a transfer: the wallet stays debited and the merchant is never credited, and nothing reports it
The ROLLBACK fails, because only the coordinator may finish its prepared transactions
quiz.why: Once rolled back, the branch is gone; the coordinator's recovery finds no prepared `txf-5@payouts` and has nothing to commit, while `wallets` committed long ago. This is the heuristic decision that breaks atomicity. Any superuser or the original user may run ROLLBACK PREPARED, so it doesn't fail. The right move was to read the log (or check `wallets`) and run COMMIT PREPARED.

quiz.q: A teammate proposes three-phase commit so that participants never block: one that hears nothing for 5 seconds will decide on its own. What does that rely on?
options: That no message or pause ever takes longer than the timeout, so silence really means the coordinator is dead
That the coordinator's log is replicated
That every participant runs the same database product
Nothing extra: the third phase removes the blocking in every case
quiz.why: 3PC's timeout rule is safe only with bounded delays. On a real network a coordinator stuck in a 6-second GC pause or behind a slow link looks dead, and participants that time out at different moments can reach different decisions. Replicating the coordinator's log with consensus is the fix that works, and it is a different design. The product doesn't matter.

quiz.q: From lesson 4: a prepared transaction has been in doubt since the weekend. On Monday, VACUUM on a busy table in the same database reports thousands of rows that "are dead but not yet removable", and the table keeps growing. Why?
options: Prepared transactions disable autovacuum until they finish
The prepared transaction counts as still running, so the removable cutoff (the horizon) can't move past its id and nothing deleted after it can be removed
The dead rows belong to the prepared transaction
VACUUM needs the row locks the prepared transaction holds
quiz.why: VACUUM removes a version only when its deleter committed before every transaction still running. A prepared transaction is still running, so the cutoff stays at its id, as the Try it showed with `removable cutoff: 767`, and every version dead since then stays. The dead rows can belong to anyone. Autovacuum still runs; it just can't remove them. That is why the PostgreSQL docs warn about leaving transactions prepared.

quiz.q: From lesson 5: two XA transactions run at once. T1 has updated a row in Oracle and now waits for a row in PostgreSQL that T2 updated. T2 now waits for T1's Oracle row. What ends this?
options: PostgreSQL's deadlock detector, after `deadlock_timeout`
Oracle's deadlock detector, which raises ORA-00060
The transaction manager, which merges both waits-for graphs
A lock or transaction timeout, because neither database sees a cycle: each sees one transaction waiting for another
quiz.why: A deadlock detector searches its own waits-for graph. PostgreSQL sees T1 waiting for T2 and nothing more; Oracle sees T2 waiting for T1. The cycle exists only across the two, and XA gives no component the whole graph, so only a timeout breaks it: a lock wait timeout on either database, or the transaction manager's own transaction timeout. Expecting a local detector to fire is the tempting mistake.

flashcards.front: What does a participant promise when it votes yes in two-phase commit?
flashcards.back: That it can and will commit if told to, even after a crash: its changes and a prepare record are on disk, it keeps its locks, and it can no longer abort on its own.

flashcards.front: What is the commit point of two-phase commit?
flashcards.back: The coordinator's decision record (`txf-1 COMMIT`) reaching its log on disk, after every yes vote and before any participant is told to commit.

flashcards.front: What does `PREPARE TRANSACTION 'gid'` do in PostgreSQL?
flashcards.back: It ends the session's transaction without finishing it: the work is saved to disk with its locks, listed in `pg_prepared_xacts`, until `COMMIT PREPARED` or `ROLLBACK PREPARED` from the same database.

flashcards.front: Why can't an in-doubt participant just roll back after a timeout?
flashcards.back: The coordinator may have decided commit and another participant may have committed already. Rolling back would leave half the transaction. So it waits, holding its locks.
A transaction with no commit record in the coordinator's log is treated as aborted. It is safe because nobody commits until that record exists.

flashcards.front: Why doesn't three-phase commit fix blocking on real networks?
flashcards.back: It is safe only if message delays and pauses are bounded. Without a bound, a slow coordinator looks dead and participants can decide differently.

flashcards.front: What does a saga give up compared with two-phase commit?
flashcards.back: Isolation and atomic commit: each step commits alone, others can see the in-between state, and undoing means running a compensating step, not a rollback.

terms.plain: Making a transaction that spans several machines commit on all of them or on none.
Prepare everywhere, record one decision durably, then commit everywhere. Not the same as two-phase locking.
The process that runs a distributed transaction, collects the votes and writes the decision.
A server that holds part of the data and votes yes or no in the prepare phase.
A participant that voted yes and hasn't learned the outcome. It can't decide alone and keeps its locks.
Treating a transaction with no commit record in the coordinator's log as aborted.
The standard interface for two-phase commit across different products, and its Java form (`XAResource`, `Xid`).
A sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating step, run by a durable workflow instead of one atomic commit.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate wants to wrap the Oracle ledger update and the IBM MQ publish in one XA transaction, "so they commit together". Explain what two-phase commit guarantees, what happens if our pod dies at the wrong moment, and what you would suggest instead.
explain_back.answer: XA runs two-phase commit with a transaction manager inside our service, Narayana in Quarkus. Both Oracle and MQ first prepare: they make the work durable, keep their locks and vote yes. Then Narayana writes one commit record to its log, and from that moment the transaction is committed; then it tells both to commit. That does make the outcome atomic. The catch is the coordinator. If the pod dies after both prepared, Oracle keeps the ledger rows locked and MQ keeps the message in limbo until Narayana comes back with the same log, and its log is on the pod's disk. If Kubernetes moves the pod to a fresh disk, a DBA has to guess the outcome, and a wrong guess breaks the very atomicity we wanted. We'd also pay extra round trips and flushes on every payment, and a deadlock between Oracle and MQ wouldn't be detected by either. Instead I'd write the ledger update and an outbox row in one local Oracle transaction, have a relay publish the outbox to the queue, and make the consumer idempotent by message id. Each piece commits locally, nothing is ever in doubt, and a crash only delays the message.

deeper.body:
**Making the coordinator survive.** Gray and Lamport's "Consensus on Transaction Commit" (2006) replaces the single coordinator's log with a group of acceptors that agree on the outcome with Paxos, so the commit decision survives as long as a majority is up. Spanner and CockroachDB take the same direction: every participant is itself a replicated group, so a participant never disappears and the coordinator's state is replicated with it. The Consistency and consensus track builds the consensus part.

**Shortcuts real transaction managers take.** If only one resource is enlisted, there is nothing to coordinate: JTA commits it in one phase, `XAResource.commit(xid, true)`. A branch that changed nothing can vote read-only (`XA_RDONLY`) in prepare and skip phase two. Some managers support a "last resource": a single non-XA resource that is committed in the middle, after the others prepared, which works until that commit's outcome is lost on the network.

**DynamoDB's version.** Lesson 8 of this track opens DynamoDB's transaction protocol: coordinators that record their decisions in a ledger table, and a recovery manager that hands a stalled transaction to another coordinator. It is two-phase commit with the coordinator's log stored in a replicated database instead of on one disk.

**The book's framing.** Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 8, covers atomic commit, XA and exactly-once message processing, and explains why many cloud services choose not to offer distributed transactions at all.
